passage: Supervisor's note. This week Damini, our intern, presented to the team. She talks with her whole face: eyebrows shooting up at good points, dropping low when she is serious, a lot of movement. Her colleague Ken told me afterwards that he found it dramatic, and wondered if she was annoyed at the questions. I asked Damini about it. She laughed and said her whole family talks that way, and that it means she is engaged, nothing more. Ken, who grew up in a quieter house, said his own face barely moves. I suggested they each compare with what is normal for the other person, not with their own habits. Next week I'll ask them how it went. - Tanvir

qa.q: Who found Damini's presentation style dramatic?
qa.a: Ken found it dramatic.

qa.q: What might Ken have been thinking about Damini's eyebrows?
qa.a: He wondered whether she was annoyed at the questions, reading her big brow movements against his own quiet baseline, though she meant only that she was engaged.

qa.q: What did Tanvir suggest the two interns do?
qa.a: Tanvir suggested they compare each other's expressions with what is normal for that person, instead of with their own habits.

qa.q: How might Damini see Ken's barely moving face?
qa.a: She could read it as flat or disinterested, when it is just how he normally looks, so the same mismatch works in reverse.

grounding: A person from an expressive background uses large brow movements that another finds dramatic, and baseline expressiveness differs by person.

passage: Tuesday night. Third week of living with my flatmate Parveen, and I finally worked out the eyebrows. Whenever she tells a story at dinner, her brows go up so high they nearly touch her hair, then crash down when she gets to the serious bit. For two weeks I thought she was always shocked or angry with me. Tonight I asked, "Are you cross?" She burst out laughing. "No! That's just how I talk. My whole family does it." She said she'd noticed my face stays very still and had wondered if I was bored. We agreed to stop guessing. Funny how one flat face and one lively one can each feel like a complaint. - Imran

qa.q: Which week of living with the flatmate is it for Imran?
qa.a: It is Imran's third week of living with the flatmate Parveen.

qa.q: What did Imran think Parveen's eyebrows meant at first?
qa.a: Imran thought she was always shocked or angry with Imran, until asking her.

qa.q: What could Imran and Parveen do to avoid misreading each other?
qa.a: They could keep checking with a quick question and remember each other's usual level of expression instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did Parveen see Imran's still face?
qa.a: She wondered if Imran was bored, so Imran's still face gave her the same kind of wrong reading that Imran had made of her.

grounding: A person from an expressive family uses big eyebrow movements while talking, another finds them dramatic, and baselines differ.

passage:
Salma had moved from Lucknow to teach in a village school near Bahraich for her fellowship year. Her co-teacher, Nazia, had the liveliest face Salma had ever seen. When Nazia talked, her eyebrows flew up, crashed down, twisted into knots.
In the first staff meeting, when Salma suggested a new reading corner, Nazia's brows shot up and pulled together at once. Salma's heart sank. She was sure Nazia hated the idea.
But Nazia said, "Yes! And we can use the old sacks as cushions!"
Over the next week, Salma watched. Nazia's brows moved like that for good news, bad news, jokes, and tea. The only time they stayed still was when a parent shouted at her about fees. Then her face went flat and quiet.
Salma learned to read Nazia against Nazia, not against her own quieter family. Still brows meant trouble. Flying brows meant Nazia.

qa.q: What did Nazia suggest using as cushions?
qa.a: The old sacks.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling in the first staff meeting when Nazia's brows moved?
qa.a: Salma felt anxious and discouraged, sure that Nazia hated the reading-corner idea.

qa.q: What did Salma learn to do that helped her read Nazia correctly?
qa.a: She learned Nazia's baseline, noticing that lively brows were normal and still brows signalled real trouble.

qa.q: How might Nazia see her own lively face?
qa.a: To Nazia it is simply how she talks, for good news, jokes and tea alike, not a sign of drama or disapproval.

grounding: The scene shows a highly expressive person's big eyebrow movements being misread, and a colleague comparing against what is normal for her.

passage:
In the student kitchen at Uppsala University, Oskar was trying to decide if his flatmate Omar was angry with him.
Omar was telling the story of his train delay, and his eyebrows were doing gymnastics: shooting up, knitting together, lifting one at a time. To Oskar, whose family barely moved their faces, it looked like fury.
"Sorry," Oskar said. "Did I do something?"
Omar stopped mid-sentence. "What? No! I'm telling you about the train."
"Your eyebrows looked very... upset."
Omar laughed so hard he had to sit down. "This is my normal face. My mother talks the same way. If I'm angry, I go quiet and my face goes stone."
Oskar thought about it. The one time Omar had been really upset, when his phone was stolen, his face had been completely still.
"So stone face is your angry face."
"And yours is your happy face," Omar grinned.

qa.q: What was Omar telling Oskar about?
qa.a: The story of his train delay.

qa.q: What was Oskar feeling while watching Omar's eyebrows?
qa.a: Oskar felt uneasy and worried, mistaking the lively eyebrows for fury.

qa.q: What helped Oskar read Omar more accurately?
qa.a: Asking directly, and remembering that Omar's face went still only when he was really upset, so comparing against Omar's own normal.

qa.q: How does Omar see Oskar's quiet face?
qa.a: Omar jokes that Oskar's still face is his happy face, showing each reads the other's baseline differently.

grounding: The scene shows big eyebrow movements from an expressive person misread as anger, and learning to compare against each person's normal.

passage: On his second day as an intern at the Bengaluru design studio, Ujjwal showed a logo draft to Joseph, the senior designer. Joseph's eyebrows shot up to his hairline. "Hmm. The orange. Interesting." Up again. Then down, then one up and one down. Ujjwal's stomach dropped. Was that disgust? Shock? Was he being mocked? He spent lunch redrawing the whole thing in grey. At four, Ritika from accounts passed his desk and saw the pile of discarded sketches. "Joseph?" she guessed. "Watch him order tea. His eyebrows do that for chai. His whole family talks like that; I met them at his wedding. Compare him with Joseph, not with you." Ujjwal watched. When the tea boy arrived, Joseph's eyebrows leapt exactly as high: "Ginger? Wonderful!" Ujjwal laughed out loud, walked over and asked him directly. "Oh, I liked the orange," Joseph said, brows dancing. "Keep it."

qa.q: What colour did Ujjwal redraw the logo in?
qa.a: Ujjwal redrew the whole thing in grey.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when Joseph's eyebrows shot up?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt anxious and deflated, reading the eyebrows as disgust or mockery, when they were really Joseph's normal lively way of talking.

qa.q: What helped Ujjwal read Joseph more accurately?
qa.a: Comparing Joseph's eyebrows with Joseph's own baseline, like when ordering tea, and then asking directly about the orange.

qa.q: How did Ritika see Joseph's eyebrows?
qa.a: Ritika knew them as Joseph's everyday style, even for chai, so she didn't read anything dramatic into them.

grounding: It shows one person's big eyebrow movements being read as dramatic by a newcomer, and learning to compare against that person's own normal.
